screens.title: Maintain Desired State with State Manager and Patch Manager
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why enforcing a desired configuration is essential for secure, reliable operations and how two Systems Manager features—State Manager and Patch Manager—achieve that automatically. Configuration drift happens gradually when manual fixes, inconsistent deployments, or missed updates change servers from their intended baseline. State Manager prevents drift by linking a declarative SSM document to target instances through an association and running that policy on a schedule. Patch Manager complements this by automating approved operating system and application updates using patch baselines, patch groups, and maintenance windows to keep systems compliant without surprising users. You will see concrete examples: a YAML SSM document that ensures a package and service are present, a step-by-step lab to create an Apache installation association, and recommended safe practices such as testing documents on non-production hosts and using maintenance windows. We’ll also cover how to monitor compliance and generate reports to satisfy audits. By the end, you should be able to design associations and patching policies that reduce operational overhead and tighten security. Consider: what would change in your environment if instances always returned to a defined, audited state?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Maintain Desired State

screens.narratorSegment: This extended objectives slide highlights practical controls and safety practices you must master. You will learn to test SSM documents using Run Command on a single non-production instance before creating an association. That small step prevents unintended disruptions. This split reduces blast radius and gives you reproducible evidence of compliance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Learning Objectives — Extended
Testing & Safety Practices
  • Test SSM documents with Run Command on non-production instances before creating associations to avoid unintended configuration changes.
  • Use patch baselines to explicitly approve or reject patches; maintain separate baselines per environment for different risk tolerances.
  • Tag instances into patch groups to scope updates and schedule them with maintenance windows during off-peak times.
  • Include pre- and post-patching steps, such as snapshots and health checks, to enable safe rollbacks and validation.
Practical pattern
Create a staging patch group and apply a new baseline there first. After successful validation, associate the baseline with production patch groups. This reduces blast radius and creates an audit trail.
Common mistake
Creating an association without testing the document can cause repeated unwanted changes. Always test first.
Pro tip
Use short schedules for testing, then lengthen them for production to balance responsiveness and load.

screens.title: What is Configuration Drift?
screens.narratorSegment: Configuration drift is the gradual divergence of a system’s state from a defined baseline. It happens when manual interventions, ad hoc troubleshooting, unattended updates, or inconsistent deployment practices change packages, services, or permissions on individual hosts. The important point is that drift is often silent: one server might have a different package version or a stopped monitoring agent and operators won’t notice until an incident or audit. Detecting drift requires a clear definition of the desired state and a mechanism to compare actual state to that definition. State Manager expresses the desired state as an SSM document and continuously evaluates and reapplies it according to the configured schedule. A concrete example: you require a monitoring agent installed on production instances. If someone stops or removes that agent on one host, that host will stop reporting, and monitoring alerts could be missed. With an association that runs hourly and ensures the agent is installed and running, State Manager will detect the difference on the next run and reinstall or restart the agent. A common misconception is that drift only matters for configuration files; in truth, drift can affect running services, installed package versions, file permissions, and scheduled jobs. The key takeaway: define a clear desired state, test your SSM document in non-production, and let State Manager continuously correct deviations so your fleet remains predictable and auditable.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Configuration drift is deviation from a baseline; prevent it by defining desired state with SSM documents and enforcing via State Manager associations.

content.html:
Core Concept › Configuration Drift
Configuration Drift
When actual system state diverges from the intended baseline.
Why it occurs
  • Manual troubleshooting that changes packages or services.
  • Ad hoc updates or missed deployments on some hosts.
  • Different runbooks or inconsistent automation across teams.
Concrete example
If a monitoring agent is stopped on a host, State Manager can detect and reapply the desired configuration to reinstall or restart it on its next scheduled run.
Key Takeaway

Drift is silent but remediable: define the desired state and use State Manager associations to enforce it continuously.

Analogy
Think of a desired state as a recipe and drift as a cook who adds the wrong spice to a single serving. State Manager is the head chef who periodically checks each plate and corrects the seasoning.
Common misconception
Drift only affects files. In reality, services, package versions, and runtime configurations all drift. Enforcement must cover installation and runtime state.
Check your understanding
  • Can you name a scenario where drift would cause a security issue?
  • How would you test an SSM document to ensure it repairs the drift safely?

screens.title: State Manager Associations and SSM Documents
screens.narratorSegment: An association is the binding between a declarative SSM document and the instances you want to manage, combined with a schedule for enforcement. The document defines the desired state as steps—such as installing a package, enabling a service, or configuring a file. When you create an association you choose targets either by tags, instance IDs, or resource groups, and specify how often the document should run. For example, you can schedule AWS-ConfigureWindowsUpdate to run nightly or run a custom AWS-RunShellScript every 30 minutes for quicker remediation during testing. A concrete example from this chapter is a document that installs a package and ensures its service is enabled and started. You should always test that document with Run Command on a single non-production host. A common mistake is skipping this test and creating an association that applies an untested change fleet-wide. To design associations safely, use short schedules for staging, give your document idempotent steps so repeated execution is safe, and enable compliance reporting. The core claim: associations let you declare a desired state and have it continually enforced. How would you structure schedules and targets for a sensitive production monitoring agent so that you minimize risk while maintaining responsiveness?

keyIdea.title: Association pattern
keyIdea.text: Create idempotent SSM documents, test, then bind with an association targeting instances via tags or IDs and a safe schedule.

content.html:
Process Flow › Associations & Documents
Association steps
  1. Author an idempotent SSM document describing desired steps (install, enable, start).
  2. Test with Run Command on a single non-production instance.
  3. Create an association: choose document, targets (tags or IDs), and schedule.
  4. Enable compliance reporting and monitor executions and results.
Concrete example (YAML)
description: "Ensures a specific package is installed and its service is running."
schemaVersion: "2.2"
parameters:
  packageName:
    type: String
    description: "(Required) The name of the package to install."
  serviceName:
    type: String
    description: "(Required) The name of the service to ensure is running."
mainSteps:
  - name: installPackage
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      commands:
        - "sudo yum install -y {{packageName}}"
      timeoutSeconds: 300
    precondition:
      StringEquals:
        - platformType
        - Linux
  - name: startService
    action: aws:runShellScript
    inputs:
      commands:
        - "sudo systemctl enable {{serviceName}}"
        - "sudo systemctl start {{serviceName}}"
      timeoutSeconds: 60
    precondition:
      StringEquals:
        - platformType
        - Linux
Supporting notes
  • Make steps idempotent so repeated runs are safe.
  • Short test schedules accelerate validation; lengthen schedules for mature policies.
  • Use tags to target dynamically created instances without constant updates.
Common mistake
Skipping Run Command testing leads to unintended configuration across many hosts.
Key Takeaway

Associations enforce desired state repeatedly; test documents and prefer idempotent steps for safe automation.

screens.title: Hands-on: InstallApacheWebServer SSM Document
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a practical SSM command document that installs and starts Apache on a Linux host. The sample document uses aws:runShellScript to run package and systemctl commands. When you test with Run Command, the document runs those commands on the chosen instance and returns output to the console. Important safety points: wrap package installation in a platform precondition so it only runs on Linux, give commands reasonable timeouts, and ensure steps are idempotent—installing the package and enabling the service is safe to run multiple times. After testing, create a State Manager association that uses this document and targets your SSM-Demo-Instance. Schedule the association to run frequently for testing and then move to a production-friendly cadence. Concrete example: the document updates packages, installs httpd, enables and starts the service, and writes a small index page. A common misconception is that the association will instantly fix manual changes; it only takes effect on the configured schedule. If you stop the service manually, wait for the next run or trigger Run Command to validate remediation. Final takeaway: use Run Command for targeted testing, validate logs, then let State Manager maintain the service automatically.

keyIdea.title: Hands-on claim
keyIdea.text: Author and test an SSM document that installs and starts Apache, then create an association for continuous enforcement.

content.html:
Definition › InstallApacheWebServer Document
Document (YAML) — copy and test
schemaVersion: "2.2"
description: "Installs and starts Apache HTTP Server."
mainSteps:
  - action: aws:runShellScript
    name: installApache
    inputs:
      commands:
        - "sudo yum update -y"
        - "sudo yum install -y httpd"
        - "sudo systemctl enable httpd"
        - "sudo systemctl start httpd"
        - "echo '<h1>Hello from State Manager!</h1>' | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.html"
      timeoutSeconds: 300
    precondition:
      StringEquals:
        - platformType
        - Linux
Testing checklist
  • Run this document with Run Command on a staging instance and inspect stdout/stderr.
  • Verify /var/www/html/index.html contains the test page and httpd is active.
  • Simulate drift by stopping httpd and wait for a scheduled association run to confirm remediation.
Note
Escaping HTML in commands matters; the document writes a small index file for quick verification but always sanitize user inputs in production.
Key Takeaway

Test documents via Run Command before associations, keep steps idempotent, and validate remediation by simulating drift.

Check
After testing, create an association named ApacheWebServerConfig targeting SSM-Demo-Instance with a short schedule for validation.

screens.title: Create a State Manager Association — Lab Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through creating a State Manager association that enforces the Apache configuration. First, choose the tested SSM document and name the association clearly, for example ApacheWebServerConfig. Next, select targets — for a single instance choose it manually, or for fleets use a tag like Environment:Production. Then configure the schedule: for testing choose a short interval such as every 5 or 30 minutes, then lengthen it after you confirm stability. Enable compliance reporting so each run is tracked and visible in Systems Manager. After creating the association, monitor the Last execution time and inspect the execution output to ensure commands succeeded. A concrete verification step is to open the instance or use Session Manager to stop the httpd service. When the association runs again, it should reinstall or restart httpd and mark the instance as Compliant. A common misconception is that State Manager will detect and fix drift instantly; it fixes drift at scheduled runs or when you trigger the document via Run Command. Final takeaway: schedule thoughtfully, monitor executions, and use compliance data to prove policy enforcement during audits.

content.html:
Process Flow › Create Association Walkthrough
Step-by-step
  1. Name the association: ApacheWebServerConfig.
  2. Select the tested document: InstallApacheWebServer (or your custom document).
  3. Choose targets: select instances manually or target by tag like Environment:Production.
  4. Specify schedule: short interval for testing; longer for production.
  5. Enable compliance reporting and create the association.
Verification checklist
  • Check Last execution and view standard output to confirm commands succeeded.
  • Simulate drift by stopping the service and observe remediation on next run.
  • Confirm the instance shows Compliant in State Manager after remediation.
Safety reminder
Use short schedules only for validation, not production. Excessively frequent runs can add load and noise; balance responsiveness with operational cost.
Key Takeaway

Create clear associations, test them, and use compliance reporting to prove enforcement. Simulate drift to confirm your policy repairs as expected.

screens.title: Patch Manager Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Patch Manager automates patch scanning, downloading, and installation for operating systems and certain applications. Its core building blocks are patch baselines and patch groups. A patch baseline defines which patches are approved or rejected, allowing you to be conservative in production and more aggressive in development. Patch groups are logical collections of instances identified by tags—for example PatchGroup:Production-WebServers—that you associate with a baseline. When combined with a maintenance window, Patch Manager will scan instances in the patch group, download approved patches, and apply them during the scheduled window. A concrete scenario: you need to apply critical security updates to development Windows servers on the second Tuesday of each month. You create a baseline that approves those critical updates, tag the servers into a development patch group, and schedule a maintenance window on the specified cadence. Patch Manager will then perform the operations during that window and report compliance. A common misconception is that patching must be immediate; in reality, scheduling patch windows avoids user disruption and gives teams control. The key takeaway: use baselines to control which updates are installed, patch groups to scope targets, and maintenance windows to control timing and risk.

keyIdea.title: Patch Manager
keyIdea.text: Use patch baselines to approve/reject patches, patch groups to target instances, and maintenance windows to schedule non-disruptive updates.

content.html:
Core Concept › Patch Manager Fundamentals
Key components
  • Patch Baseline: rules that approve or reject patches.
  • Patch Group: instances grouped by tags and associated with a baseline.
  • Maintenance Window: scheduled time to run disruptive operations like patching.
Concrete scenario
Schedule critical Windows updates for development servers on the second Tuesday each month by creating a baseline that approves those security patches, tagging the servers into a PatchGroup:Dev-Windows, and scheduling a maintenance window for that cadence.
Common mistake
Applying broad baselines to production without rejecting known bad patches can lead to outages. Maintain separate baselines per environment.
Key Takeaway

Patch Manager automates safe, auditable updates when you control approvals with baselines and scope with patch groups and windows.

Monitoring
Patch Manager provides compliance reports listing compliant and non-compliant instances and patch reasons, useful for audits and troubleshooting.

screens.title: Patch Baselines and Patch Groups — Design Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Designing patching policies is about controlling risk and ensuring reproducible, auditable updates. Use patch baselines to decide which patches are acceptable in each environment. For example, production baselines may only approve critical security fixes, while development baselines can approve a broader range of updates. Patch groups are implemented by tagging instances; associate a patch group with a baseline to ensure consistent behavior across targeted instances. Maintenance windows wrap this behavior in a scheduled, non-disruptive operation window. Include pre-patch steps such as snapshots and post-patch checks that validate service health. This architecture reduces blast radius and gives you checkpoints to roll back if needed. A concrete pattern: create three baselines—strict production, standard staging, permissive development—and corresponding patch groups. Test new baselines in the development patch group first, then promote them to staging and production once validated. A common misconception is that one-size-fits-all baselines are sufficient. They are not. Environment-specific baselines combined with maintenance windows and automation steps provide safer, auditable updates and smoother incident response. The takeaway: separate approval policies by environment and automate safety checks to protect availability. Patch Baselines and Patch Groups — Design Patterns means use multiple baselines and patch groups plus maintenance windows, pre/post steps, and staged promotion for safe patching.. In practical terms, scoping updates and approvals to minimize risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture › Baselines & Patch Groups
Recommended architecture
Production Baseline
Approve critical security patches only; reject problematic or disruptive updates.
Staging Baseline
Approve a broader set of updates for validation before production rollout.
Development Baseline
More permissive approvals to catch integration issues early.
Tag instances into patch groups such as PatchGroup:Prod-Web or PatchGroup:Staging-App. Associate each group with the appropriate baseline and schedule a maintenance window. Include snapshots and health checks as automation steps to reduce rollback risk.
Practical tip
Promote baselines after successful validation in development and staging to keep production stable.
Key Takeaway

Separate baselines by environment and use patch groups plus maintenance windows to limit impact and provide auditable control.

screens.title: Monitoring Compliance and Reports
screens.narratorSegment: Both State Manager and Patch Manager provide compliance reporting that helps you prove systems meet policy. State Manager records association execution history and compliance status for each instance—Compliant or Non-compliant—along with run summaries. Patch Manager offers patch compliance reports showing which instances are missing approved patches, which patches were rejected, and the reasons. These reports are valuable during audits because they list the concrete evidence: execution timestamps, patch IDs, and remediation results. For continuous monitoring, integrate Systems Manager compliance data with AWS Config so you can aggregate and query compliance across accounts and regions. A concrete use: during an audit, run a compliance report for your production patch group to show all critical patches were applied in the last maintenance window. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safety Notes
screens.narratorSegment: A handful of recurring mistakes create most SSM and patching pain. First, applying untested SSM documents fleet-wide can cause repeated disruptions. Always test with Run Command on a single non-production instance and inspect outputs. Second, using a single baseline for all environments ignores different risk tolerances; separate baselines for production, staging, and development reduce incidents. Third, skipping maintenance windows allows updates to run at inconvenient times; schedule windows during off-peak hours. Fourth, not including pre- and post-patching automation such as snapshots and health checks increases rollback complexity. Practical example: for patching, take instance snapshots before applying updates during a maintenance window so you can recover quickly if a patch causes instability. A misconception is believing State Manager alone guarantees safety; it guarantees enforcement, not correctness. That’s why testing, staged promotion, and automated validation are mandatory. The core takeaway: combine testing, targeted baselines, maintenance windows, and automation steps to maintain both stability and compliance while minimizing operational risk. screens.title: Parameter Store vs Secrets Manager (Supporting Topic)
screens.narratorSegment: Maintaining desired state often relies on storing configuration values and secrets securely. Two services covered in the source are SSM Parameter Store and AWS Secrets Manager. Parameter Store provides hierarchical parameters and supports String, StringList, and SecureString, which uses KMS encryption. It's an efficient choice for static configuration values and some secrets using SecureString. Secrets Manager specializes in credential management with automatic rotation for supported services, versioning of secrets, and a richer audit trail. Choose Parameter Store for cost-effective static configuration and Secrets Manager for credentials that require frequent, automatic rotation. A concrete example: store a database connection string as a SecureString parameter for environment configuration, but store rotating database credentials in Secrets Manager so automatic rotation reduces exposure from long-lived credentials. A common misconception is that SecureString is equivalent to Secrets Manager; while both encrypt values, Secrets Manager provides rotation and advanced secret lifecycle features. The takeaway: pick the service that matches your rotation and audit needs, and integrate secure retrieval into SSM documents or application startup so desired state enforcement has the right secrets at runtime. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why enforcing a desired configuration is essential for secure, reliable operations and how two Systems Manager features—State Manager and Patch Manager—achieve that automatically. Configuration drift happens gradually when manual fixes, inconsistent deployments, or missed updates change servers from their intended baseline. State Manager prevents drift by linking a declarative SSM document to target instances through an association and running that policy on a schedule. Patch Manager complements this by automating approved operating system and application updates using patch baselines, patch groups, and maintenance windows to keep systems compliant without surprising users. You will see concrete examples: a YAML SSM document that ensures a package and service are present, a step-by-step lab to create an Apache installation association, and recommended safe practices such as testing documents on non-production hosts and using maintenance windows. We’ll also cover how to monitor compliance and generate reports to satisfy audits. By the end, you should be able to design associations and patching policies that reduce operational overhead and tighten security. Consider: what would change in your environment if instances always returned to a defined, audited state?

In this chapter we focus on four measurable skills you will practice and verify. First, you will configure SSM State Manager to enforce a desired configuration across managed instances. That means authoring an SSM document and creating an association with a schedule and targets so a policy is applied repeatedly. Second, you will understand configuration drift: what causes it, how State Manager detects and corrects it, and the operational benefits of continuous enforcement. Third, you will implement Patch Manager to automate operating system patching, including creating patch baselines and defining which patches are approved or rejected. Finally, you will define patch groups and associate them with baselines, schedule maintenance windows for non-disruptive updates, and monitor patch compliance using Systems Manager reporting and AWS Config. Each objective includes a competency milestone so you can verify results during the hands-on activity and assessment steps.

This extended objectives slide highlights practical controls and safety practices you must master. You will learn to test SSM documents using Run Command on a single non-production instance before creating an association. That small step prevents unintended disruptions. You will also learn to create patch baselines that approve critical security updates while rejecting known problematic patches, and to associate patch groups using tags so you can target environments like production or development separately. Finally, you will practice configuring maintenance windows and pre- and post-patching automation steps, such as snapshots or health checks, to reduce rollback risk. These capabilities together deliver predictable change management. A useful habit is to keep a short test window where a new baseline is applied to a staging patch group; if it behaves, then roll it out to production. This split reduces blast radius and gives you reproducible evidence of compliance.

Configuration drift is the gradual divergence of a system’s state from a defined baseline. It happens when manual interventions, ad hoc troubleshooting, unattended updates, or inconsistent deployment practices change packages, services, or permissions on individual hosts. The important point is that drift is often silent: one server might have a different package version or a stopped monitoring agent and operators won’t notice until an incident or audit. Detecting drift requires a clear definition of the desired state and a mechanism to compare actual state to that definition. State Manager expresses the desired state as an SSM document and continuously evaluates and reapplies it according to the configured schedule. A concrete example: you require a monitoring agent installed on production instances. If someone stops or removes that agent on one host, that host will stop reporting, and monitoring alerts could be missed. With an association that runs hourly and ensures the agent is installed and running, State Manager will detect the difference on the next run and reinstall or restart the agent. A common misconception is that drift only matters for configuration files; in truth, drift can affect running services, installed package versions, file permissions, and scheduled jobs. The key takeaway: define a clear desired state, test your SSM document in non-production, and let State Manager continuously correct deviations so your fleet remains predictable and auditable.

An association is the binding between a declarative SSM document and the instances you want to manage, combined with a schedule for enforcement. The document defines the desired state as steps—such as installing a package, enabling a service, or configuring a file. When you create an association you choose targets either by tags, instance IDs, or resource groups, and specify how often the document should run. For example, you can schedule AWS-ConfigureWindowsUpdate to run nightly or run a custom AWS-RunShellScript every 30 minutes for quicker remediation during testing. A concrete example from this chapter is a document that installs a package and ensures its service is enabled and started. You should always test that document with Run Command on a single non-production host. A common mistake is skipping this test and creating an association that applies an untested change fleet-wide. To design associations safely, use short schedules for staging, give your document idempotent steps so repeated execution is safe, and enable compliance reporting. The core claim: associations let you declare a desired state and have it continually enforced. How would you structure schedules and targets for a sensitive production monitoring agent so that you minimize risk while maintaining responsiveness?

We'll walk through a practical SSM command document that installs and starts Apache on a Linux host. The sample document uses aws:runShellScript to run package and systemctl commands. When you test with Run Command, the document runs those commands on the chosen instance and returns output to the console. Important safety points: wrap package installation in a platform precondition so it only runs on Linux, give commands reasonable timeouts, and ensure steps are idempotent—installing the package and enabling the service is safe to run multiple times. After testing, create a State Manager association that uses this document and targets your SSM-Demo-Instance. Schedule the association to run frequently for testing and then move to a production-friendly cadence. Concrete example: the document updates packages, installs httpd, enables and starts the service, and writes a small index page. A common misconception is that the association will instantly fix manual changes; it only takes effect on the configured schedule. If you stop the service manually, wait for the next run or trigger Run Command to validate remediation. Final takeaway: use Run Command for targeted testing, validate logs, then let State Manager maintain the service automatically.

This walkthrough guides you through creating a State Manager association that enforces the Apache configuration. First, choose the tested SSM document and name the association clearly, for example ApacheWebServerConfig. Next, select targets — for a single instance choose it manually, or for fleets use a tag like Environment:Production. Then configure the schedule: for testing choose a short interval such as every 5 or 30 minutes, then lengthen it after you confirm stability. Enable compliance reporting so each run is tracked and visible in Systems Manager. After creating the association, monitor the Last execution time and inspect the execution output to ensure commands succeeded. A concrete verification step is to open the instance or use Session Manager to stop the httpd service. When the association runs again, it should reinstall or restart httpd and mark the instance as Compliant. A common misconception is that State Manager will detect and fix drift instantly; it fixes drift at scheduled runs or when you trigger the document via Run Command. Final takeaway: schedule thoughtfully, monitor executions, and use compliance data to prove policy enforcement during audits.

Patch Manager automates patch scanning, downloading, and installation for operating systems and certain applications. Its core building blocks are patch baselines and patch groups. A patch baseline defines which patches are approved or rejected, allowing you to be conservative in production and more aggressive in development. Patch groups are logical collections of instances identified by tags—for example PatchGroup:Production-WebServers—that you associate with a baseline. When combined with a maintenance window, Patch Manager will scan instances in the patch group, download approved patches, and apply them during the scheduled window. A concrete scenario: you need to apply critical security updates to development Windows servers on the second Tuesday of each month. You create a baseline that approves those critical updates, tag the servers into a development patch group, and schedule a maintenance window on the specified cadence. Patch Manager will then perform the operations during that window and report compliance. A common misconception is that patching must be immediate; in reality, scheduling patch windows avoids user disruption and gives teams control. The key takeaway: use baselines to control which updates are installed, patch groups to scope targets, and maintenance windows to control timing and risk.

Designing patching policies is about controlling risk and ensuring reproducible, auditable updates. Use patch baselines to decide which patches are acceptable in each environment. For example, production baselines may only approve critical security fixes, while development baselines can approve a broader range of updates. Patch groups are implemented by tagging instances; associate a patch group with a baseline to ensure consistent behavior across targeted instances. Maintenance windows wrap this behavior in a scheduled, non-disruptive operation window. Include pre-patch steps such as snapshots and post-patch checks that validate service health. This architecture reduces blast radius and gives you checkpoints to roll back if needed. A concrete pattern: create three baselines—strict production, standard staging, permissive development—and corresponding patch groups. Test new baselines in the development patch group first, then promote them to staging and production once validated. A common misconception is that one-size-fits-all baselines are sufficient. They are not. Environment-specific baselines combined with maintenance windows and automation steps provide safer, auditable updates and smoother incident response. The takeaway: separate approval policies by environment and automate safety checks to protect availability. A handful of recurring mistakes create most SSM and patching pain. First, applying untested SSM documents fleet-wide can cause repeated disruptions. Always test with Run Command on a single non-production instance and inspect outputs. Second, using a single baseline for all environments ignores different risk tolerances; separate baselines for production, staging, and development reduce incidents. Third, skipping maintenance windows allows updates to run at inconvenient times; schedule windows during off-peak hours. Fourth, not including pre- and post-patching automation such as snapshots and health checks increases rollback complexity. Practical example: for patching, take instance snapshots before applying updates during a maintenance window so you can recover quickly if a patch causes instability. A misconception is believing State Manager alone guarantees safety; it guarantees enforcement, not correctness. That’s why testing, staged promotion, and automated validation are mandatory. The core takeaway: combine testing, targeted baselines, maintenance windows, and automation steps to maintain both stability and compliance while minimizing operational risk. Maintaining desired state often relies on storing configuration values and secrets securely. Two services covered in the source are SSM Parameter Store and AWS Secrets Manager. Parameter Store provides hierarchical parameters and supports String, StringList, and SecureString, which uses KMS encryption. It's an efficient choice for static configuration values and some secrets using SecureString. Secrets Manager specializes in credential management with automatic rotation for supported services, versioning of secrets, and a richer audit trail. Choose Parameter Store for cost-effective static configuration and Secrets Manager for credentials that require frequent, automatic rotation. A concrete example: store a database connection string as a SecureString parameter for environment configuration, but store rotating database credentials in Secrets Manager so automatic rotation reduces exposure from long-lived credentials. A common misconception is that SecureString is equivalent to Secrets Manager; while both encrypt values, Secrets Manager provides rotation and advanced secret lifecycle features. The takeaway: pick the service that matches your rotation and audit needs, and integrate secure retrieval into SSM documents or application startup so desired state enforcement has the right secrets at runtime.
